content.title: About
content.content: Frozen corn that has been pre‑cooked with vegetable oil is a convenient ready‑to‑heat product. Corn provides carbohydrates, dietary fiber, and a modest amount of protein, while the added oil boosts its energy content and flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the world’s most widely cultivated grain crops.
Freezing preserves most B‑vitamins and antioxidants such as lutein.
Cooking with oil improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins, including vitamin A present in corn.
Corn is commonly used as a side dish, in salads, soups, and Asian stir‑fries.
There are several corn varieties: sweet, yellow, white, and semi‑white.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Readily digestible carbohydrates supply quick energy, useful for active lifestyles.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin help protect eye health against age‑related changes.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin, and folate aid in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: The added vegetable oil provides omega‑6 fatty acids.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The oil increases the product’s calories, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to corn.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions contain added salt; check the label if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: Corn has a moderate glycemic index, which can affect blood sugar levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen corn in the microwave, on a skillet, or in a steamer for 3‑5 minutes. Serve as a side dish, add to salads, soups, tacos, or vegetable mixes. Sprinkle with fresh herbs, cheese, or your favorite spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package in the freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once opened, use within 1‑2 months. Do not thaw and keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

frozen-coffee-drink-decaffeinated-nonfat.title: Frozen Coffee Drink, Decaffeinated, Nonfat, with Whipped Cream

content.title: About
content.content: A frozen coffee beverage made from roasted coffee beans but without caffeine. The drink is nonfat, and a light whipped cream topping adds a smooth, creamy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually done by water or CO₂ methods, preserving aromatic compounds.
Nonfat dairy reduces calories while maintaining a creamy texture thanks to the airy foam.
Frozen coffee drinks are popular in hot climates as a refreshing dessert.
Whipped cream is added just before freezing to keep a light structure.
Often served in cafés as a “frappe” without added sugar.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: The nonfat formula and lack of added sugar make it suitable for weight management.

items.title: Coffee antioxidants
items.content: Even without caffeine, the drink retains polyphenols that support cellular health.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Light whipped cream may contain small amounts of probiotic cultures that benefit gut flora.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A frozen beverage provides extra fluid intake during warm weather.

items.title: Caffeine‑free
items.content: Ideal for individuals sensitive to caffeine or who need to avoid it for medical reasons.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Whipped cream can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: If sweetened, the drink’s glycemic index and calorie count increase.

items.title: Improper storage temperature
items.content: Incorrect freezing can cause crystallization and texture changes.

items.title: Possible artificial flavorings
items.content: Some manufacturers use synthetic flavorings that may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve immediately after thawing in a glass; you can add fresh berries or mint for extra aroma. Optionally sprinkle cinnamon or cocoa powder on top.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a freezer at –18 °C in an airtight package. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours, otherwise the texture may deteriorate.

pizza-cheese-from-school-lunch-thick-cru.title: Cheese Pizza, School Lunch, Thick Crust

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese pizza is a popular school lunch option, made on a thick, crunchy crust. The dough typically contains wheat flour, yeast, water and salt, topped with tomato sauce and shredded cheese that melts into a golden layer.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A thick crust makes the pizza more filling and holds more sauce.
The cheese used in school pizzas is often a blend of mozzarella and cheddar for better melt and flavor.
Tomato sauce in school pizzas is usually made from tomato paste, salt and a modest amount of spices.
Pizza is included in school nutrition programs in many countries as a source of carbs and calcium.
Traditionally the pizza is cut into 6–8 triangular slices, which are easy for children to handle.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cheese topping provides calcium, essential for growing bones and teeth in children.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Cheese and any added meat supply animal protein that supports growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: The crust delivers complex carbohydrates that give sustained energy for the school day.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes and yeast in the dough contain B1, B2 and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene
items.content: Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may help protect cells.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in children with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce and cheese often contain added salt, so intake should be moderate, especially for children with hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The thick crust and cheese make the pizza calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended to avoid over‑eating.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat flour dough contains gluten, which can be problematic for children with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pizza is usually served hot, cut into triangular slices. It can be topped with fresh vegetables or herbs for added nutrition. Children may eat it with their hands or use a fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover pizza in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

pork-potatoes-and-vegetables-including-c.title: Pork, potatoes, and vegetables with gravy

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of tender pork, boiled or roasted potatoes, and a mix of vegetables – carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens (spinach, kale). It is served with a savory gravy made from meat stock and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide.
Potatoes are a primary source of carbohydrates in many diets.
Broccoli is rich in vitamin C and compounds that support detoxification.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables provide high amounts of vitamin K and folate.
Gravy made from meat stock enhances iron absorption from pork.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Pork supplies complete animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: The meat contains thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Heme iron from pork is more readily absorbed, especially when paired with vitamin C from broccoli.

items.title: Potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potatoes and leafy greens are rich in potassium and magnesium, helping maintain normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene in carrots and polyphenols in broccoli help combat free radicals.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Some cuts of pork can be fatty; choose lean cuts and trim excess fat.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Prepared gravies often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Pork must be cooked thoroughly to eliminate salmonella and trichinella.

items.title: Allergy to certain vegetables
items.content: Rarely, individuals may react to broccoli or leafy greens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot: place sliced pork alongside potatoes and vegetables, then drizzle with gravy. Garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers within two hours, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze for 1‑2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked seaweed with added fat is a marine plant that has been blanched and then lightly fried in a small amount of vegetable oil. It has a tender texture, a mildly salty sea flavor, and a subtle aroma. The product is commonly used in Asian cuisine as a side dish, salad ingredient, soup garnish, or sushi wrap.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Seaweeds are among the oldest living organisms on Earth, existing for over 600 million years.
More than 10,000 seaweed species are known, but edible varieties most often include kelp, nori and wakame.
Frying in oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin D and carotenoids.
Seaweeds are a rich natural source of iodine, essential for thyroid hormone production.
In Japan, cooked seaweed is traditionally served with soy sauce and vinegar as a snack called “okonomiyaki”.

items.title: High in iodine
items.content: Iodine supports the synthesis of thyroid hormones that regulate metabolism.

items.title: Source of polysaccharides
items.content: Polysaccharides like alginates help maintain a healthy gut microbiota.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Seaweed provides vitamin E, carotenoids and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: The polyunsaturated fats from the added oil may help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Calcium, magnesium, iron and potassium in seaweed are important for bones, muscles and nerve function.

items.title: Excess iodine
items.content: Consuming too much iodine can disrupt thyroid function, especially in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cooked seaweed is often salted; people monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to marine algae.

items.title: Contaminants
items.content: Seaweed can accumulate heavy metals and toxins from the ocean; choose products from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked seaweed with fat can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, soups, rice or noodle dishes, and used as a wrapper for sushi rolls. It is easy to slice into strips or pieces. Serve with a drizzle of soy sauce or a sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product in a sealed container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. It usually stays fresh for 7–10 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor, discoloration, or visible mold.
